title: What Is Logic?
summary: Discover what logic means, why it matters, and how logical thinking helps us reach conclusions based on evidence rather than guesses.
learningObjectives: Recognize the difference between reasoning and guessing
Identify the basic steps used in logical thinking
Explain why conclusions must be supported by information

contentBlocks.content: Logic is a disciplined way of thinking. It helps us examine information, identify relationships and reach conclusions that are supported by the available facts.

contentBlocks.title: Key idea
contentBlocks.content: Logical thinking does not ask whether an answer merely sounds believable. It asks whether the answer is properly supported by the information given.
A guess may be based on instinct, personal experience or incomplete information. A logical conclusion is reached by carefully examining the facts and applying a valid reasoning process.

contentBlocks.title: Example
contentBlocks.content: Statement: All mangoes in this basket are ripe. This fruit came from the basket. Conclusion: The fruit is ripe. The conclusion follows because it is supported by both pieces of information.

contentBlocks.title: Do not add information
contentBlocks.content: You cannot conclude that the fruit is sweet, large or yellow. Those details were not provided, even though they may be true in real life.

items: Identify the facts that are given.
Choose the conclusion supported by the facts.

contentBlocks.title: Think about it
contentBlocks.content: A conclusion appears sensible, but one important fact required to prove it is missing. Is the conclusion logically established? No. A sensible possibility is not necessarily a valid conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson summary
contentBlocks.content: Logic helps us reach conclusions through evidence and valid reasoning. We must use the information provided, distinguish reasoning from guessing and avoid adding unstated facts.

contentBlocks.title: Key takeaways
items: Logic is disciplined and evidence-based thinking.
A valid conclusion must be supported by the given information.
A believable statement is not automatically a logical conclusion.
Never introduce facts or assumptions that the question does not provide.
